'''Lloyd Steadman Nelson''' (March 29, 1922 – August 28, 2013) was an American statistician. He is known for developing the [[Nelson rules]], a [[statistical process control]] methodology to determine when a process is out of control.

==Early life==
Lloyd Steadman Nelson was born on March 29, 1922, in [[Norwich, Connecticut]], to Marion (née Rogers) and Ronald R. Nelson.<ref name="obit">{{Cite news |url=https://www.legacy.com/us/obituaries/ctpost/name/lloyd-nelson-obituary?id=19885473 |title=Dr. Lloyd S. Nelson |date=2013-09-08 |newspaper=Connecticut Post |via=legacy.com |access-date=2025-06-20}}</ref><ref name="birth">{{Cite news |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-day-class-baby-hostess-at-supper-to/174938120/ |title=Class Baby Hostess at Supper to Members of Mother's Class |date=1924-06-09 |newspaper=The Evening Day |page=5 |via=[[Newspapers.com]] |access-date=2025-06-20}}{{Open access}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-day-marion-nelson-in-colleges-1st/174938559/ |title=Marion Nelson in College's 1st Class, Dies |date=1968-10-02 |newspaper=The Day |page=35 |via=[[Newspapers.com]] |access-date=2025-06-20}}{{Open access}}</ref> He graduated from the [[University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill]] with a [[Bachelor of Science]] in chemistry in 1943.<ref name="obit"/><ref>{{Cite news |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-charlotte-observer-earn-degrees-at-u/174939132/ |title=Earn Degrees at University |date=1943-09-05 |newspaper=[[The Charlotte Observer]] |page=8 |via=[[Newspapers.com]] |access-date=2025-06-20}}{{Open access}}</ref> He served in the [[United States Navy]] from 1944 to 1946. He then graduated with a [[Doctor of Philosophy|PhD]] in inorganic chemistry from the [[University of Connecticut]] in 1950.<ref name="obit"/><ref name="asq">{{Cite web |url=https://asq.org/about-asq/honorary-members/nelson?srsltid=AfmBOooFn2DG4gx169MkO3R9nwuU8VIXI2v-dq24pshkdKM1tN5PxZTX |title=Dr. Lloyd S. Nelson |website=[[American Society for Quality]] |access-date=2025-06-20}}</ref>

==Career==
Nelson taught for a few years.<ref name="obit"/> He was a consulting statistician with [[GE Lighting|General Electric Lamp Division]] in [[Cleveland]]. He was then manager at the Applied Mathematics Laboratory at [[GE Appliances]] in [[Louisville, Kentucky]].<ref name="asq"/> In 1980, he began working for [[Nashua Corporation]] as director of statistical methods. In 1992, he retired from Nashua Corporation.<ref name="obit"/><ref name="asq"/>

Nelson was editor of the [[American Society for Quality]] (ASQ) publication ''Industrial Quality Control'' in the 1960s and helped direct the publication to split into two, a general interest magazine ''Quality Progress'' and a technical quarterly publication the ''Journal of Quality Technology''. He was the first editor of the ''Journal of Quality Technology''.<ref name="asq"/> He served on ASQ's awards board and the Shewhart and Deming Medal committees. He was a member of the ''Journal of Quality Technology'''s editorial review board. He wrote the "Technical Aids" feature of the ''Journal of Quality Technology'' for more than 20 years.<ref name="asq"/>

In the October 1984 issue of the ''Journal of Quality Technology'', Nelson first published the [[Nelson rules]], a [[statistical process control]] methodology to indicate when a process is out of control.<ref>{{Cite book |url=https://archive.org/details/isbn_9781323401163/page/500/mode/2up |title=Thinking Like An Engineer: An Active Learning Approach |last=Stephan |first=Elizabeth A. |year=2015 |pages=500–502 |via=[[Archive.org]] |access-date=2025-06-20}}</ref><ref>Lloyd S. Nelson, "The Shewhart Control Chart—Tests for Special Causes". Journal of Quality Technology 16, no. 4 (October 1984), 238-239. https://doi.org/10.1080/00224065.1984.11978921</ref>

==Personal life==
Nelson married Frances "Fran" Betty Pallant, daughter of Margaret (née Roth) and Frank W. Pallant, in 1982.<ref name="obit"/><ref name="wife">{{Cite news |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-courier-journal-nelson-francis-bett/174937761/ |title=Nelson, Francis Betty Pallant |date=2007-07-29 |newspaper=[[Courier Journal]] |page=B7 |via=[[Newspapers.com]] |access-date=2025-06-20}}{{Open access}}</ref> They had one son and two daughters, Peter R., Fay and Barbara.<ref name="obit"/> His wife died in 2007.<ref name="wife"/> He lived most of his life in [[Londonderry, New Hampshire]].<ref name="obit"/>

Nelson died on August 28, 2013, in [[Clemson, South Carolina]].<ref name="asq"/>

==Awards and legacy==
In 1964, Nelson was made a fellow of ASQ and was awarded the [[Shewhart Medal]] in 1978. In 2001, he received ASQ's Distinguished Service Medal.<ref name="asq"/> On February 8, 2003, he was made an honorary member of ASQ.<ref name="asq"/> Subsequently, to commemorate his many contributions, the [[Lloyd S. Nelson Award]] was established in his honor.<ref>{{cite journal |title=Robert Mee Receives the Lloyd S. Nelson Award |journal=Journal of Quality Technology |volume=38 |issue=4 |pages=384 |date=October 2006 |url=https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/pdf/10.1080/00224065.2006.11918591 |quote=This award was instituted in 2003 to commemorate the many contributions of Dr. Nelson to JQT and ASQ.}}</ref>

In [[W. Edwards Deming]]'s ''[[Out of the Crisis]]'', Deming highlights Nelson's observation that "the most important figures that one needs for management are unknown or unknowable, but successful management must nevertheless take them into account".<ref name="asq"/>
